See how this bachelor compares with study options at UCR

This is a pre-produced programme comparison. Your search helped you find the programme; it did not personalize the comparison.

← Back to search

Maastricht Arts and Culture studies contemporary cultural and societal questions through history, philosophy, art, literature and qualitative social research. It connects art, science and technology, media and politics through content courses, paired skills and an individual thesis.

Three qualified UCR alternatives approach cultural history and the arts, digital culture and ethics, or environmental culture and governance. Each has substantive related study and different companion subjects. Maastricht’s integrated methods and research sequence remain distinct.

Academic year: 2026–2027

This 180 EC illustration selects Othering Europe, Power and Democracy, Analysing Arts II and Doing Conceptual Analysis II from restricted menus. Open 30 EC occurs in Year 3, semester 5. Progression, attendance and elective approvals apply; English research and writing lead to an English proposal and thesis.

What this comparison shows

A curriculum-level comparison of Arts and Culture at Maastricht University (Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences) with 3 illustrative UCR study compositions.

CLOSEST UCR MATCH
Culture, history, philosophy and the arts

History, philosophy, literary interpretation, art and qualitative research anchor this cultural-studies response. Rhetoric and political/social perspectives add context. Ancient archaeology and warfare history contribute specific historical subjects; they do not reproduce Maastricht’s integrated methods, paired skills modules or thesis.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Digital culture, media and ethics

Media archaeology, film, screens, art and literature combine with ethics and philosophy of mind and self. Data handling, databases and machine learning add technical tools. Those tools and business and economic study do not supply cultural theory, ethnography or Maastricht’s integrated research sequence.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Environmental culture, media and governance

Media representation, climate communication, social movements and sustainability governance frame environmental questions. Climate science, water management, circularity and geochemistry add disciplinary background. Scientific coherence does not make those subjects cultural analysis; the humanities, media and governance contributions provide this qualified response.

Important limitation

This is a curriculum comparison. A UCR composition is not the same disciplinary degree and does not by itself establish a professional qualification or automatic eligibility for a particular master’s programme.

Rows show curricular relationships, including partial matches, rather than course equivalence. A blank cell means there is no closely comparable component in that row. Optional independent research is additional to the displayed 180 EC.

modals.text:
Personal & Professional Development
This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
Close

Business & Economy in the Age of AI
As we enter the “Age of AI,” this course explores AI’s business, managerial, economic, and societal implications. It is designed for UCR students with a strong interest in AI and requires no prior technical background. The course traces AI’s evolution from early research to generative AI, highlighting its capabilities and limits. Through real-world examples and business cases, students analyse AI’s impact on competitiveness, innovation, labour markets, economic growth, inequality, climate change and society. In this context, students critically examine AI governance and ethics, addressing issues such as bias, privacy, and fairness across business functions (e.g. Marketing, HR, Finance), while also exploring corporate governance and regulation more broadly.
Close

AI Ethics
AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility, accountability, the moral status of AI systems and broader political risks. Students also consider trust and decision-making, empathy and confidentiality in clinical settings, algorithmic stereotypes, and how AI companions and tutors may affect children’s learning and relationships.
Close

Database Management Systems
Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
Close

Introduction to Data Science
Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
Close

Machine Learning
Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Real-world examples illustrate the methods, their strengths and limitations.
Close

Neural Networks & Deep Learning
Neural Networks & Deep Learning combines theory with practical Python implementations. Students build and train networks, use TensorFlow, and study applications to tabular data, computer vision and text classification. Recent language-model developments are discussed; image-generation models may be considered if time permits.
Close

Mathematical Methods
Mathematical Methods develops foundational techniques in differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations. Students solve mathematical problems and apply these techniques in projects drawing on fields such as science, economics and sociology.
Close

Living with Water
Studies water risks and opportunities in deltas, including flood protection, freshwater management, salinisation, subsidence and governance. Readings, discussions and real-world cases examine nature-based adaptation and resilient planning; guest contributions and field activities in Zeeland may be included.
Close

Governance of Sustainability
This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
Close

Environmental Biogeochemistry
Examines soil, mineral, rock and water interactions, biological and chemical controls on mineral formation, nutrient and metal adsorption and leaching, wastewater treatment and resource recovery. Uses geochemical modelling, exercises and a case study; laboratory experiments may be included.
Close

Sustainability Essentials I
Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries: the environmental limits within which human development can take place. It provides foundations for further study in the Environment and Sustainability cluster.
Close

Sustainability Essentials II
Develops physical-science foundations for sustainability through waves, chemistry and materials science. Reflective work and a project apply these topics to analysing greenwashing.
Close

Climate Change
Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
Close

Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
Close

Research in a Sustainable Delta
In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor
Close

Law, Society & Justice
Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students explore legal systems and fields including constitutional, administrative, criminal and international law, human rights and selected private-law topics. Case law and trial simulations support discussion of law, society and justice.
Close

Modern History
Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
Close

Western Way of War
Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.
Close

Native American Histories
Native American Histories studies Indigenous history and life from the nineteenth to the twenty-first century. Work with Indigenous students, scholars and elders addresses boarding schools, human trafficking, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, cultural resistance and regeneration. Indigenous methodologies emphasise storytelling, reciprocity and relational knowledge; gender studies, psychology and sociology help connect past and present.
Close

History Research Seminar
Investigates the 1809 Walcheren Expedition through primary sources, including diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports from different participants. Students learn to find, read and analyse historical evidence and write a substantial research paper, with considerable independent study.
Close

Introduction to Public International Law
Introduction to Public International Law examines the creation and historical development of international law, its sources, subjects and organisation. Topics include the use of force, armed conflict, international criminal law, refugees and environmental law, followed by self-determination, Third World Approaches and treaty politics. Assessment includes exercises, exams, a podcast and reflection.
Close

Foundations of European Union Law
Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
Close

Introduction to Western Philosophy
Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
Close

Ethics
Ethics examines virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism, alongside moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Students apply ethical arguments to issues including equality, poverty and wealth, animal rights, future generations, climate change and historical injustice. Papers and presentations develop independent argumentation.
Close

Philosophy of Mind
Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
Close

Free Will, Time & the Self
Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.
Close

Introduction to Political Philosophy
Introduction to Political Philosophy examines influential Western thinkers from classical antiquity to the present. Students study views of human nature, society and political authority, place theories in their historical settings and compare their arguments and proposed solutions with contemporary political problems.
Close

European Union Politics
European Union Politics examines EU actors, institutions and decision-making rules. Students study how state and non-state interests shape policy and conduct group research on a legislative dossier, interest groups and Members of the European Parliament using the EU transparency register.
Close

Peace & Conflict
Peace & Conflict introduces theories about the causes, consequences and possible resolution of violent and nonviolent conflicts. Historical and contemporary cases address structural inequality, ideology, humiliation and colonial or postcolonial grievances. Students compare international, institutional, cultural and civil-society perspectives and examine how concepts such as justice, truth and reconciliation travel between fields.
Close

Qualitative Research Methodology
Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
Close

Social Movements & Environmental Justice
Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
Close

New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
Close

The Art of Rhetorical Communication
The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.
Close

Communicating the Climate Crisis
Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.
Close

Rhetoric in Action
Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
Close

Persuasive Communication
Persuasive Communication builds on classical rhetoric and argumentation to study persuasion in science, society and sustainability. Students examine framing, nudging, cognitive shortcuts and ethical approaches to persuasion. In a community-engaged project, they help local institutions address communication challenges.
Close

Creative Communication Laboratory
Creative Communication Laboratory combines critical reading, theory, discussion and reflective writing with poetry, rhythm, sound, voice and performance. Students develop poetic and hybrid creative projects. Singing, songwriting and music performance are excluded; sound must function as poetic, linguistic or conceptual material.
Close

Introduction to Western Art History
Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from the early Renaissance to the present. Key paintings, artists and movements introduce visual analysis and interpretation. The course also considers how institutions, markets, critics and historiographers shape the understanding and legacy of artworks.
Close

Introduction to World Archaeology
Introduction to World Archaeology explores craft production and material culture in ancient societies around the world. Students examine how making objects relates to religious, social and gendered identities, technologies and environmental effects. An experimental educational activity and discussion of contemporary archaeological methods connect interpretation with practice.
Close

Greek Archaeology
Explores the archaeology of community and democracy in early-democratic Greece, seeking ancient lessons on community decision-making.
Close

Modern Art & Modern Museums
Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
Close

Introduction to Literary Studies
Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.
Close

Life & Travel Writing
Life & Travel Writing examines memoir, autobiography, diaries, personal essays, travel narratives and blogs in literature and popular culture. Students analyse autobiographical media and theories of life narrative, develop writing, presentation and debating skills, and create structured personal narratives informed by their own experience.
Close

Film & Text
Film & Text studies relationships between literary and film narratives, adaptation and intertextuality. Students learn methods of film analysis and examine plot, character, setting, image, acting, music and sound, alongside the relationships among adaptors, critics and viewers.
Close

Introduction to Film & Media
Introduction to Film & Media focuses primarily on cinema history, film culture and analysis. Students study narrative, cinematography, editing and sound, examine influential films in their theoretical and political contexts, and engage with academic readings. The final part briefly connects film to television, streaming and digital platforms.
Close

Media Archaeology
Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
Close

From T.V. to TikTok
From T.V. to TikTok examines American social history and everyday life through mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Television, film, podcasts and social media reveal how storytelling constructs identity and possible futures. Native American and disability representation illustrate how media can marginalise and empower people.
Close

Media & the Environment
Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
Close

The Documentary
Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
Close

These qualified responses retain genuine cultural, historical, philosophical, literary and media analysis. Technical computing, organizational study and environmental science are companion subjects, not substitutes for cultural theory. Maastricht’s ethnography, discourse and conceptual-analysis progression and 16 EC thesis remain different.

Maastricht combines content courses with separately credited skills and a scaffolded proposal/thesis sequence. UCR distributes related work across whole courses; optional independent research is additional to the scheduled 180 EC. Neither its different format nor thematic similarity establishes degree or professional equivalence.

modals.text:
Personal & Professional Development
This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
Close

Business & Economy in the Age of AI
As we enter the “Age of AI,” this course explores AI’s business, managerial, economic, and societal implications. It is designed for UCR students with a strong interest in AI and requires no prior technical background. The course traces AI’s evolution from early research to generative AI, highlighting its capabilities and limits. Through real-world examples and business cases, students analyse AI’s impact on competitiveness, innovation, labour markets, economic growth, inequality, climate change and society. In this context, students critically examine AI governance and ethics, addressing issues such as bias, privacy, and fairness across business functions (e.g. Marketing, HR, Finance), while also exploring corporate governance and regulation more broadly.
Close

AI Ethics
AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility, accountability, the moral status of AI systems and broader political risks. Students also consider trust and decision-making, empathy and confidentiality in clinical settings, algorithmic stereotypes, and how AI companions and tutors may affect children’s learning and relationships.
Close

Database Management Systems
Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
Close

Introduction to Data Science
Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
Close

Machine Learning
Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Real-world examples illustrate the methods, their strengths and limitations.
Close

Neural Networks & Deep Learning
Neural Networks & Deep Learning combines theory with practical Python implementations. Students build and train networks, use TensorFlow, and study applications to tabular data, computer vision and text classification. Recent language-model developments are discussed; image-generation models may be considered if time permits.
Close

Mathematical Methods
Mathematical Methods develops foundational techniques in differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations. Students solve mathematical problems and apply these techniques in projects drawing on fields such as science, economics and sociology.
Close

Living with Water
Studies water risks and opportunities in deltas, including flood protection, freshwater management, salinisation, subsidence and governance. Readings, discussions and real-world cases examine nature-based adaptation and resilient planning; guest contributions and field activities in Zeeland may be included.
Close

Governance of Sustainability
This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
Close

Environmental Biogeochemistry
Examines soil, mineral, rock and water interactions, biological and chemical controls on mineral formation, nutrient and metal adsorption and leaching, wastewater treatment and resource recovery. Uses geochemical modelling, exercises and a case study; laboratory experiments may be included.
Close

Sustainability Essentials I
Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries: the environmental limits within which human development can take place. It provides foundations for further study in the Environment and Sustainability cluster.
Close

Sustainability Essentials II
Develops physical-science foundations for sustainability through waves, chemistry and materials science. Reflective work and a project apply these topics to analysing greenwashing.
Close

Climate Change
Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
Close

Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
Close

Research in a Sustainable Delta
In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor
Close

Law, Society & Justice
Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students explore legal systems and fields including constitutional, administrative, criminal and international law, human rights and selected private-law topics. Case law and trial simulations support discussion of law, society and justice.
Close

Modern History
Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
Close

Western Way of War
Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.
Close

Native American Histories
Native American Histories studies Indigenous history and life from the nineteenth to the twenty-first century. Work with Indigenous students, scholars and elders addresses boarding schools, human trafficking, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, cultural resistance and regeneration. Indigenous methodologies emphasise storytelling, reciprocity and relational knowledge; gender studies, psychology and sociology help connect past and present.
Close

History Research Seminar
Investigates the 1809 Walcheren Expedition through primary sources, including diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports from different participants. Students learn to find, read and analyse historical evidence and write a substantial research paper, with considerable independent study.
Close

Introduction to Public International Law
Introduction to Public International Law examines the creation and historical development of international law, its sources, subjects and organisation. Topics include the use of force, armed conflict, international criminal law, refugees and environmental law, followed by self-determination, Third World Approaches and treaty politics. Assessment includes exercises, exams, a podcast and reflection.
Close

Foundations of European Union Law
Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
Close

Introduction to Western Philosophy
Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
Close

Ethics
Ethics examines virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism, alongside moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Students apply ethical arguments to issues including equality, poverty and wealth, animal rights, future generations, climate change and historical injustice. Papers and presentations develop independent argumentation.
Close

Philosophy of Mind
Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
Close

Free Will, Time & the Self
Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.
Close

Introduction to Political Philosophy
Introduction to Political Philosophy examines influential Western thinkers from classical antiquity to the present. Students study views of human nature, society and political authority, place theories in their historical settings and compare their arguments and proposed solutions with contemporary political problems.
Close

European Union Politics
European Union Politics examines EU actors, institutions and decision-making rules. Students study how state and non-state interests shape policy and conduct group research on a legislative dossier, interest groups and Members of the European Parliament using the EU transparency register.
Close

Peace & Conflict
Peace & Conflict introduces theories about the causes, consequences and possible resolution of violent and nonviolent conflicts. Historical and contemporary cases address structural inequality, ideology, humiliation and colonial or postcolonial grievances. Students compare international, institutional, cultural and civil-society perspectives and examine how concepts such as justice, truth and reconciliation travel between fields.
Close

Qualitative Research Methodology
Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
Close

Social Movements & Environmental Justice
Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
Close

New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
Close

The Art of Rhetorical Communication
The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.
Close

Communicating the Climate Crisis
Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.
Close

Rhetoric in Action
Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
Close

Persuasive Communication
Persuasive Communication builds on classical rhetoric and argumentation to study persuasion in science, society and sustainability. Students examine framing, nudging, cognitive shortcuts and ethical approaches to persuasion. In a community-engaged project, they help local institutions address communication challenges.
Close

Creative Communication Laboratory
Creative Communication Laboratory combines critical reading, theory, discussion and reflective writing with poetry, rhythm, sound, voice and performance. Students develop poetic and hybrid creative projects. Singing, songwriting and music performance are excluded; sound must function as poetic, linguistic or conceptual material.
Close

Introduction to Western Art History
Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from the early Renaissance to the present. Key paintings, artists and movements introduce visual analysis and interpretation. The course also considers how institutions, markets, critics and historiographers shape the understanding and legacy of artworks.
Close

Introduction to World Archaeology
Introduction to World Archaeology explores craft production and material culture in ancient societies around the world. Students examine how making objects relates to religious, social and gendered identities, technologies and environmental effects. An experimental educational activity and discussion of contemporary archaeological methods connect interpretation with practice.
Close

Greek Archaeology
Explores the archaeology of community and democracy in early-democratic Greece, seeking ancient lessons on community decision-making.
Close

Modern Art & Modern Museums
Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
Close

Introduction to Literary Studies
Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.
Close

Life & Travel Writing
Life & Travel Writing examines memoir, autobiography, diaries, personal essays, travel narratives and blogs in literature and popular culture. Students analyse autobiographical media and theories of life narrative, develop writing, presentation and debating skills, and create structured personal narratives informed by their own experience.
Close

Film & Text
Film & Text studies relationships between literary and film narratives, adaptation and intertextuality. Students learn methods of film analysis and examine plot, character, setting, image, acting, music and sound, alongside the relationships among adaptors, critics and viewers.
Close

Introduction to Film & Media
Introduction to Film & Media focuses primarily on cinema history, film culture and analysis. Students study narrative, cinematography, editing and sound, examine influential films in their theoretical and political contexts, and engage with academic readings. The final part briefly connects film to television, streaming and digital platforms.
Close

Media Archaeology
Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
Close

From T.V. to TikTok
From T.V. to TikTok examines American social history and everyday life through mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Television, film, podcasts and social media reveal how storytelling constructs identity and possible futures. Native American and disability representation illustrate how media can marginalise and empower people.
Close

Media & the Environment
Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
Close

The Documentary
Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
Close
